ca_basalt_boulders.blurb:
A shoreline boulder field on the Palos Verdes coast, tucked into Pelican Cove below the cliffs. The stone is dark, solid basalt, with columns in places and a honeycomb of pockets in others. Most of the problems are easy to moderate, with plenty of VB to V2 and only a handful harder, so it suits beginners and anyone wanting a mellow session by the ocean.

Landings are usually over rocks, water or both, so bring pads and a spotter. The tide matters: high water can cut off the boulders, so time your visit for a lower tide. The walk along the beach is short and the boulders are in view the whole way.
ca_basalt_boulders.parking_note: Use the large paved lot just off Palos Verdes Drive South, roughly half a mile beyond the Point Vicente Lighthouse.
ca_basalt_boulders.approach: From the lot on the bluff, descend the steep path to the sand, then head right along the water. The boulders come into view as you walk.

ca_psycho_boulders.blurb:
A concentrated cluster of granite boulders in the Quail Springs part of Joshua Tree, hidden in a quiet little valley behind a larger formation. It packs a lot of good problems into a small space, from beginner cracks and slabs up through a solid block of V3 and V4 problems, with a few harder lines above that.

The walk in is about a quarter hour on trail and then a short scramble, so it feels more secluded than the roadside areas, and this corner of the park tends to be lightly visited. Bring pads for the landings.
ca_psycho_boulders.approach: From the Quail Springs parking area, follow the trail toward Baskerville Rock and go around the left side of it. Take the first spur off to the right, climb the slope, bear right at the top and keep the rocks on your right until you are behind the formation. The big Psycho Boulder is on your left.

ca_n_sentinel_creek_area.blurb:
A shady, secluded stretch of the south side of Yosemite Valley, just right of Sentinel Rock. The climbing is almost all traditional crack and corner climbing, with a couple of bolted lines, and the grades cluster in the 5.10s with a good number of 5.11s above them. Popular lines include Manana, Vanishing Point, Mental Block, Hari-Kiri and Yin-Yang.

Because the walls sit in shade, it works well on warm days. Expect a short approach on the Valley Loop Trail followed by a steep climbers' path, and carry a full trad rack. Parking along the road is tight.
ca_n_sentinel_creek_area.parking_note: Pull into the curbed turnouts along Southside Drive near the Four Mile Trailhead. Space is limited, so arriving by the Valley shuttle is often easier.
ca_n_sentinel_creek_area.approach: Take the connector from the turnout to the Valley Loop Trail, then watch for the climbers' trail that leaves it at a carabiner sign just past an obvious stone step. It leads to the base of Manana.

ca_wheeler_gorge.blurb:
A roadside canyon crag in the Los Padres hills north of Ojai, with mostly bolted sport routes spread over several neighboring walls that each have their own feel, from smooth and featureless to pocketed. The grades are generally on the soft side and the protection is good, which makes it a friendly place to step up into the 5.10s and 5.11s. Favorites include Silent Mind, Blush, Danger Boy, Economique, Goulara and Sick Boy.

The gorge is deeply shaded and the creek keeps it cool in summer, but winter days are cold because little sun reaches the walls. High creek flow can cut off some routes.
ca_wheeler_gorge.parking_note: Park in one of the pullouts beside Highway 33, about seven miles north of the junction with Highway 150 in Ojai, near the pair of tunnels. Mind the traffic.
ca_wheeler_gorge.approach: Walk through the first tunnel to the bridge, then follow the climbers' trail down toward the creek.

ca_hideout_the.blurb:
A small, tight cluster of boulders in an oak woodland outside Ojai, with excellent rock quality and the problems close enough together that one pad session covers a lot. The grades run from easy up through V8 but most of the problems sit between V0 and V5. Force of Magic, North Face and The Phage are among the best.

The oaks keep it cool in hot weather, though the same shade leaves the boulders wet for a long time after a storm, so give it several days to dry. The nearby trail is busy with hikers, runners and bikers, so plan on a modest hike in.
ca_hideout_the.approach: Two ways in. The Pratt Trail is slightly gentler and shadier: follow it about a mile, then Foothill Road and a dirt road past a gate and water tank, cross the dry creek and take the right-hand trail. Alternatively park where the road ends at the gate, walk the dirt road to the kiosk, climb the Fox Canyon Trail about a mile and take the left fork.

ca_lower_dinosaur_rock_corridor.blurb:
A tidy little slot between two facing walls on the Lower Dinosaur Rock formation, in the pines of the San Bernardino Mountains above Running Springs at around 6,300 feet. It holds a mix of trad lines and a few bolted routes on a south-facing wall and a north-facing one, so you can pick sun or shade. Most of the climbing falls between 5.7 and 5.10, with a few harder routes.

The rock around Dinosaur Rocks is notably sharp, so tape up before jamming cracks. Reaching the corridor takes a bit of scrambling around the base of the north face.
ca_lower_dinosaur_rock_corridor.parking_note: Take Keller Peak Road, which leaves Highway 18 about a mile east of Running Springs. The trail starts at a roadside campsite where space is limited, so use the small pullout opposite if the site is taken.
ca_lower_dinosaur_rock_corridor.approach: Starting from the east, work uphill around the foot of the north side to where the corridor opens. There is some easy scrambling on the way.

ca_mystery_science_theater.blurb:
The main crag on Conejo Mountain, above Newbury Park, and the first wall you reach along the service road. The routes are short and pumpy on steep to slabby volcanic rock, mostly sport with a scattering of trad and top-rope lines, and many fall in the 5.9 to 5.11 range. Are You Happy in Your Work?, The Beginning of the End and the easy Push the Button Frank are good places to start.

The wall faces east and gets afternoon shade. Rock quality is poor in spots, with loose blocks, so wear a helmet and test holds. Give it a couple of days to dry after rain.
ca_mystery_science_theater.parking_note: Park on Lesser Street, a turn off Reino Road in Newbury Park, short of the yellow fire hydrant. The trailhead is across the street, between two houses. Keep noise down; it is a residential street.
ca_mystery_science_theater.approach: Follow the trail uphill from between the houses and continue to the first crag along the service road.

ca_east_wall.blurb:
The far end of the main formation at Lover's Leap, a big wall of vertical cracks crossed by horizontal dikes that give rests and holds. The East Wall is classic moderate trad climbing, with most routes in the 5.8 to 5.10 range and a few harder ones. Standouts include The Line, Bear's Reach, Fantasia, Scimitar, East Crack and Fear No Evil.

The wall is the farthest of the four from the campground, which tends to thin out the crowds, but the main walls do get busy on summer weekends. Most multipitch routes are best finished by walking off.
ca_east_wall.parking_note: From South Lake Tahoe drive about 18 miles west on Highway 50 to Strawberry and turn off just before the lodge. Use the main lot by the trailhead.
ca_east_wall.approach: Leave from the back of the lot on the broad, well-kept Pioneer Trail, which reaches the base of the formation in under twenty minutes.

ca_mammoth_crest.blurb:
A quiet alpine wall at about 10,200 feet above McLeod Lake, above Mammoth Lakes, visible from the Lake Mary and Horseshoe Lake area. The routes are mostly trad and alpine-style, with a few bolted lines, and the grades concentrate in the 5.10s with some 5.9s and 5.11s. Plum Line, Flower Power, Sierra Slam and A Good Ribbing are among the favorites.

Most of the wall faces north to northeast, with sun roughly from early morning to early afternoon in high season. The path up from the lake is well marked, but the altitude and the hike mean a committing day.
ca_mammoth_crest.parking_note: Drive Highway 203 toward Lake Mary and continue past the turnoff to the large Horseshoe Lake lot.
ca_mammoth_crest.approach: Take the Mammoth Pass Trail to McLeod Lake and pass around the right side. Near the southwest shore, enter the trees and follow the worn path, then a smaller trail, up the hillside to the rocks.

ca_ice_caves.blurb:
The cave-like chambers within the Sad Boulders, in the Volcanic Tablelands north of Bishop. The tuff is steep and powerful, and the problems here run harder than most of the tablelands: a few V0 to V3 warm-ups, then a deep run of V4 and above, with Cream Horn, Mothership Connection, The Ninth Wave and Beefcake among the best known.

The low, dark chambers stay cool and shaded even on warm days, which makes this a good refuge when the rest of Bishop is hot. Bring plenty of pads.
ca_ice_caves.parking_note: From US 395 north of Bishop, turn onto Pleasant Valley Dam Road, pass the county campground, then follow Chalk Bluff Road about 4.5 miles to the Sad Boulders parking area.
